newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish King lashes out at ETA over killing.
newsitem.headline: Spanish King lashes out at ETA over killing.

text.p: Spain's King Juan Carlos lashed out on Wednesday at ETA Basque guerrillas, branding them "contemptible terrorists" for their killing of a young Spanish politician.
It was one of the strongest condemnations of the separatist rebels by the king, who normally tries to stay out of politics.
"His murder was as contemptible as the terrorists who killed him," the king said during a speech in Berlin which was broadcast on Spanish national radio.

The king added his voice to a nationwide outcry against ETA for its abduction and killing of 29-year-old Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco after the government refused the group's demand for a transfer of prisoners.
Millions of Spaniards vented their rage with unprecedented force in four straight days of mass protests across the country. The killing was strongly condemned around the world.
The government said it knew the demonstrations were a call for action against the separatists and vowed to crack down.
A leading Basque nationalist politician said on Wednesday that ETA had committed political suicide with the killing.
Inaki Anasagasti, chief spokesman for the the Basque Nationalist Party, said that while many Basques shared the dream of an independent homeland, they strongly repudiated ETA after the latest attack.

"ETA has committed suicide because they are left without any support in the streets, they are left without any justification for their actions," Anasagasti told state television. His moderate party is the leading political force in the Basque country of northern Spain.
Anasagasti said ETA had now completely lost the "romantic image" that attracted many young Basques to its cause, beginning in the 1960s under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.
Huge crowds of demonstrators took to the streets overnight in several major cities in the fourth day of angry protests.
In the northeastern city of Zaragoza, Blanco's grieving family led hundreds of thousands in a protest march.
"I will only say that if the death of my son has served to unite the Basque country, Spain and the whole world and it ends all the bad in the world, my son's death is welcome," Blanco's mother said.

France's Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou denounced the murder of Blanco and pledged to expedite the handing over of ETA members wanted in Spain. The rebels have traditionally used southwest France as a base for attacks across the border.

The public outcry did not deter the guerrillas from issuing a death threat against a second Basque politician, 63-year-old Jose Luis Caso. The Basque town councillor in Renteria has been protected by bodyguards since the threat was made on Monday.
Caso, like Blanco, is a member of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party.

The killing of an ordinary, low-ranking official stunned Spaniards and marked a crucial turning point in public opinion. Basques once intimidated by ETA are now boldly confronting its supporters in a drive to isolate them.
An opinion poll taken after Blanco's kidnapping but before his death showed 66 percent of Spaniards support the conservative government's refusal to negotiate with ETA.
ETA has killed nearly 800 people in its 29-year struggle for a Basque homeland.
While protests overnight were mostly peaceful, gatherings in some cities in the Basque region once again turned violent.
In Bilbao, ETA opponents threw stones and bottles at offices and bars used by the rebel group's political wing, Herri Batasuna. One ETA supporter was arrested during the clashes.
